name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season. Right now it's after harvest, so I'm out drilling winter wheat with the old John Deere, the one without all the screens. We grow wheat, barley and oilseed rape, that's the yellow crop they crush for cooking oil, on about two hundred hectares round Hilltop Farm, and keep a few cattle on the rough ground. My wife Greta keeps the house and does the farm accounts, and on Sundays we're at church in the village with the boys. I like a straight row and a full grain store. I don't like forms, and I don't like being told how to farm by people who've never done it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Does the farm use much technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Less than most round here. The neighbours have tractors that steer themselves by satellite, and good luck to them. I steer my own. I've never used one of these AI chat things and I don't see why I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a tool, leave it at that. People get carried away with every new gadget. I'd say it after church over coffee, and most of the men would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing. Wheat grows the same whether there's AI on a computer or not. What matters is the weather, the price at harvest and the cost of fertiliser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Sell the grain in spring when the price is usually better, if the store holds. Put a bit aside for a new trailer, about eight thousand, which I've been saving for since last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Nothing to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try it, even once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My eldest, Jakob, tried to show me on his phone. It wrote me a poem about a tractor. Very nice, I said, now help me with the drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about, if not this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fertiliser price, honestly. It doubled two years ago and we nearly didn't spread on the barley. Nobody in the city noticed, but it nearly cost us the year.

S0.say: It's a tool, so leave it at that. People get carried away with every new gadget, and most of the men after church would agree.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, because wheat grows the same either way. What matters is the weather, the harvest price and the cost of fertiliser.
S0.do: Sells the grain in spring when prices are usually better and keeps saving for a new trailer at about eight thousand. Changes nothing else on the farm.
S0.quote: It wrote me a poem about a tractor. Very nice, I said, now help me with the drill.
S0.fieldNote: He was short and dismissive, though the story of his son's poem made him smile. His real worries are fertiliser prices and the weather. He frames community through church and the opinions of the men he drinks coffee with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies hiring fewer young people is wrong, a young man needs work to become a man. Bring back proper apprenticeships, paid by the businesses, not the government. That's what I'd say, and I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow suits me fine. I'll farm the way I farm. But Jakob is sixteen and doesn't want the farm, he wants to be an engineer, and if firms take on fewer beginners, he'll struggle to get his start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jakob to look for an apprenticeship now, with the agricultural engineering firm in town, not a university. I'd ask Mr Weber who runs it whether he'd take a lad. On the farm, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the farm. A bit uneasy about the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather Jakob took the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But I'd never force him. My father forced me a bit, and I've been grateful and resentful in about equal parts. Our younger one, Lukas, might want it, he's twelve and already drives the quad better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should pay for apprenticeships, if not the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies who need the workers. If you want a skilled man later, you train a boy now. The government should get out of the way and maybe give a tax break, that's all.

S1.say: Companies hiring fewer young people is wrong, because a young man needs work. Bring back proper apprenticeships, paid by businesses, not the government.
S1.think: Slow suits me fine, and I'll farm my way. But my son Jakob wants to be an engineer, and fewer beginner jobs would make his start hard.
S1.do: Pushes sixteen-year-old Jakob toward an apprenticeship at the agricultural engineering firm in town instead of university. Asks Mr Weber, who runs it, to take him on, and leaves the farm unchanged.
S1.feel: Calm about the farm and a little uneasy about his son.
S1.quote: My father forced me a bit, and I've been grateful and resentful in about equal parts.
S1.fieldNote: His worry is for his son's start, which he'd fix through local connections rather than the state. The admission about his own father was surprisingly open. He clearly hopes his younger boy Lukas might take the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government shouldn't bail out every office worker, people need to stand on their own feet. Find another job, learn a trade, the way farmers always have when times are hard. I'd say it on the farming forum, and I'd get some stick for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not as hard as I sound. Greta's sister works in a bank in the city, and if she lost her job I'd want her looked after. I'd help her myself before I'd want the government doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Greta's sister she can stay with us if it comes to that, there's a spare room. I'd keep the savings, about four months, and not touch them. And I'd ask the grain merchant whether the price is going to move, because if all the trading goes to computers, I want to know who's on the other end of the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should stand on their own feet, but you'd take in Greta's sister. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Family looks after family, that's how it should work. It's the government doing it for strangers that I don't like, because then nobody looks after anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the new AI jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. I'd sooner drive a lorry. But for a young person who's good with computers, fine, if it's real work and not just sitting at home.

S2.say: The government shouldn't bail out every office worker; people need to stand on their own feet. Find another job or learn a trade, the way farmers always have.
S2.think: I'm not as hard as I sound, and I'd want Greta's sister looked after if she lost her bank job. I'd rather help her myself than have the government do it.
S2.do: Offers his sister-in-law the spare room if needed and keeps the four months of savings untouched. Asks the grain merchant whether prices will move if trading goes to computers.
S2.feel: Uneasy, mostly for family rather than himself.
S2.quote: Family looks after family, that's how it should work. It's the government doing it for strangers that I don't like, because then nobody looks after anybody.
S2.fieldNote: There was a clear gap between his tough public line and his private soft spot for his sister-in-law. When I named it, he resolved it through his belief that family, not the state, should care for people. He would sooner drive a lorry than take an AI job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built it should keep what they earn, but they should pay their fair taxes like anyone else. I don't like the shouting about taking it off them. A crisis is a crisis, but you don't fix it by punishing success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, grain is fine, people need bread. But if share prices and house prices go mad, it'll come back on us through land prices and rents. And if the city goes into crisis, the government will come looking for money, and farmers are always an easy target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the grain early, while prices are steady, and not gamble on spring. I'd pay off the last bit of the machinery loan, about twelve thousand, so we owe nobody but the bank for the house. And I'd pray a bit harder on Sundays, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a little angry. It's other people's mess landing on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pray harder. What would you pray for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady hands for the people in charge, and for the boys to find good work. I don't pray for the price of wheat, my mother said that was greedy. I just pray for the strength to take whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell any land if prices went sky-high?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My grandfather bought the first fields in 1961. I'm not the one who sells them, whatever someone offers.

S3.say: The people who built it should keep what they earn but pay their fair taxes. You don't fix a crisis by punishing success.
S3.think: Grain is fine, because people need bread. But booming prices come back on us through land and rents, and in a crisis the government always comes for farmers.
S3.do: Sells grain early while prices are steady and pays off the last twelve thousand of the machinery loan. Prays harder on Sundays, and refuses to sell any land.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a little angry that other people's mess is landing on him.
S3.quote: I don't pray for the price of wheat, my mother said that was greedy. I just pray for the strength to take whatever comes.
S3.fieldNote: He became more reflective here, especially about faith, and his line about his mother was quietly moving. His instinct is to clear debts and hold land, the opposite of a gamble. He sees government, not AI, as the bigger threat to farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are a step too far, and the companies pushing them don't know the land. I'd say the government shouldn't subsidise them. Let the market decide, and I'd bet a lot of farmers say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one frightens me. A combine that drives itself, a sprayer that runs all night, and the big farms would buy them and grow grain cheaper than I ever can. I've got my old John Deere, and I'm not changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Greta about whether we rent some land out to the neighbour with the self-driving kit, while still farming the rest ourselves. I'd look at the cattle side more, because robots on hill pasture seem far off. And I'd sit the boys down and tell them the truth, that the farm might look different by the time they're grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep well. It feels like the world's moving on and leaving me in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the boys exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, your great-grandfather bought this land with his hands, and your father farmed it with his. I don't know what you'll farm it with. But it's still ours, and we don't sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said let the market decide. But the market might choose robots. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose, I suppose. I believe in the market, but I didn't think it would come for me. That's a hard thing to say out loud.

S4.say: Robots on farms are a step too far, and the companies pushing them don't know the land. The government shouldn't subsidise them; let the market decide.
S4.think: Self-driving combines and sprayers would let big farms grow grain cheaper than I ever can. I've got my old John Deere and I'm not changing.
S4.do: Talks with Greta about renting some land to the neighbour with self-driving kit while farming the rest. Leans more on the cattle, and tells his sons honestly that the farm may look different by the time they're grown.
S4.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, as if the world is moving on and leaving him in the yard.
S4.quote: I believe in the market, but I didn't think it would come for me. That's a hard thing to say out loud.
S4.fieldNote: When I gently pointed out that the market he trusts might choose robots, he admitted it, and it clearly hurt. He would rather rent land out than change his own machinery. Keeping the land in the family is the line he won't cross.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help isn't handouts, it's being left alone with fair rules. Stop the government paying the big farms to buy robots, and keep the grain markets honest, so a small farmer gets a fair price.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the church and the village. If the farms go to robots, there's nobody in the pews, nobody at the school. The village dies, and that's not something you can put a price on.

headlineQuote: I believe in the market, but I didn't think it would come for me.
portrait: Karl is a 43-year-old grain and oilseed farmer on two hundred hectares at Hilltop Farm, married to Greta, with two sons and a strong attachment to church and village. He steers his own old tractor, has never used AI and believes in free markets, family support and apprenticeships over government help. In the early scenarios he's calm, though privately he'd take in his sister-in-law and worries about his son's first job. The robot scenario alarms him most, and he admits that the market he believes in might come for him.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because self-driving combines and sprayers would let big farms grow grain far more cheaply than he can.
whatWouldHelp: Not handouts but fair rules: no government money for big farms to buy robots, and honest grain markets that give small farmers a fair price.
